title: Ogre Aunt Brum and the Secret Paths
markdown:
High in the Whispering Peaks, where the wind sang lullabies through giant pines and moonlight painted the snow with starlight secrets, lived Ogre Aunt Brum. Immense, yes: hands like the biggest catcher’s mitts, a voice that could rumble like an avalanche and make cottage stones tremble. Yet she kept the most delicate painted porcelain teacups, and she smoothed her moss-green dress — the softest mountain moss — with surprising grace.

Her constant companion was Pudding, a huge shaggy mastiff who often looked like a walking hearth rug. When his tail thumped the stone floor it sounded like a happy drum solo. He did not bark much. He spoke with nudges, deep sighs that vibrated through the floor, and the most expressive ear twitches. Big brown eyes followed Aunt Brum. They lived quietly, with only distant mule bells and the sighing wind for company. His nose is better than any map, she liked to say, when there was no one to hear it but the teacups.

One crisp afternoon, as she polished a cup with tiny bluebirds painted on it, a shadow fell across her doorway. A traveler, windswept, kind-faced, well-worn knapsack, clearly turned around in the passes.

“Good day. I’m terribly sorry to disturb your quiet. I’m looking for Silverstream village. My map has vanished. A hermit told me an ogre might know the secret paths.”

Aunt Brum set the teacup down with a soft clink. “Silverstream. A charming village. Though the paths are, shall we say, delightfully winding.” She looked at the rugged mountains. “I usually stick to my herb garden. Fear not. We’ll get you safely on your way.”

From the hearth Pudding rumbled agreement and padded over, cool damp nose to her hand.

“Pudding knows the general direction. His nose is better than any map for finding the true way. Adventurous, mind you. We’ll manage.”

Cucumber sandwiches, dainty as only Aunt Brum could pack them, and a thermos of chamomile. They set off. The air grew colder. The path became a thin ribbon clinging to the mountainside between crags that scraped the sky. Mule bells returned, lonely. Aunt Brum moved with surprising graceful ease. Pudding trotted ahead, nose to ground, an occasional soft whine she understood perfectly.

At a confusing fork a small whiskered head popped from a pile of rocks: Pipkin the Marmot, known for loud cheerful whistles and for appearing when least expected, usually at inconvenient moments. Jaunty whistles. He darted up a high rock, chattering as if sharing urgent news.

“Oh, botheration,” Aunt Brum sighed, voice soft and musical. “Pipkin. Always something to say when we need to concentrate. He’s pointing — but I’m not sure if it’s the right way, or just pointing for the sake of it.”

The traveler looked bewildered. “He just looks like he’s being a marmot.”

“Indeed. His timing is highly suspect. Dramatic appearances precisely when the decision is most crucial.”

The path split again: one route so steep it looked like a goat trail, the other vanishing into a shadowy ravine. Aunt Brum hesitated. Pudding whined, nudging toward the ravine’s darkness. Pipkin whistled urgently and mimed climbing, pointing up.

Just as she was about to follow the miming, thick swirling fog descended, wrapping the mountains in an opaque shroud, erasing the path, muffling sound. “Most inconvenient. Now we truly cannot see a thing.”

Pudding, usually so calm, whimpered, magnificent ears drooping. He looked from her troubled face to Pipkin and back, then nudged with more urgency and a soft distressed growl, soulful eyes fixed on the marmot.

Aunt Brum paused. Pudding was not only distressed by fog. He was distressed by Pipkin’s unwavering persistence. And marmots, she knew from hours of watching, were not usually the type to offer unsolicited directional advice.

“Pudding. Is Pipkin trying to warn us away from that steep path?”

A small affirmative woof. A nudge toward the ravine. Pipkin’s long high whistle: not a direction. A note of alarm.

“You know,” Aunt Brum said, a slow knowing smile, “Pipkin has always been a creature of dramatic flair. Perhaps his whistles aren’t directions but observations. And perhaps that path isn’t as safe as it looks. And this ravine is perhaps the true way forward.” She took a steadying breath. “Right then, Pudding. His nose is better than any map. Lead on, my dear boy.”

Pudding puffed with quiet pride and set off into the ravine, senses sharper than any traveler’s in thick fog. They followed. As they descended the fog thinned. Below, in a hidden cleft, a powerful waterfall tumbled into a crystalline pool. Last wisps of mist danced. Falling water caught faint ethereal moonlight and became a cascading curtain of liquid silver.

The ravine path, less obvious than the one Pipkin had indicated, was the correct route. It led them at last to the edge of Silverstream, where the stream’s murmur was the most welcome sound. The traveler’s thanks warmed Aunt Brum more deeply than any mug of her special tea.

Back in the cottage she poured a steaming cup. Pudding curled by the crackling fire, tail a soft rhythmic thump-thump. She did not explain the journey to the bluebirds on the porcelain. She only listened to the drum of that tail, and to the wind in the pines, which had gone back to lullabies. The next day Silverstream would hear, and there would be bread and berry pies. For now the teacup steamed, the hearth glowed, and Pudding’s nose, better than any map, twitched once in sleep toward the door they no longer needed to open.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
